claim: Vertebrate limb morphology often reflects the environment due to variation in locomotor requirements.
source: Vertebrate limb morphology often reflects the environment due to variation in locomotor requirements.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding about limb morphology and locomotion.

claim: Proximal and distal limb segments may evolve differently from one another, reflecting an anatomical gradient of functional specialization.
source: However, proximal and distal limb segments may evolve differently from one another, reflecting an anatomical gradient of functional specialization that has been suggested to be impacted by the timing of development.
evidence: This statement is presented as a hypothesis that has been suggested in the literature, indicating it is based on prior research and inference.

claim: The anatomical gradient of functional specialization has been suggested to be impacted by the timing of development.
source: However, proximal and distal limb segments may evolve differently from one another, reflecting an anatomical gradient of functional specialization that has been suggested to be impacted by the timing of development.
evidence: This claim references a hypothesis from prior literature about developmental timing affecting functional specialization.

claim: The study explores whether the temporal sequence of bone condensation predicts variation in the capacity of evolution to generate morphological diversity in proximal and distal forelimb segments across more than 600 species of mammals.
source: Here, we explore whether the temporal sequence of bone condensation predicts variation in the capacity of evolution to generate morphological diversity in proximal and distal forelimb segments across more than 600 species of mammals.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's research question and sample size.

claim: Distal elements exhibit greater shape diversity than intermediate and upper limb segments.
source: Distal elements not only exhibit greater shape diversity, but also show stronger within-element integration and, on average, faster evolutionary responses than intermediate and upper limb segments.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Distal elements show stronger within-element integration than intermediate and upper limb segments.
source: Distal elements not only exhibit greater shape diversity, but also show stronger within-element integration and, on average, faster evolutionary responses than intermediate and upper limb segments.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Distal elements show, on average, faster evolutionary responses than intermediate and upper limb segments.
source: Distal elements not only exhibit greater shape diversity, but also show stronger within-element integration and, on average, faster evolutionary responses than intermediate and upper limb segments.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Results are consistent with the hypothesis that late developing distal bones display greater morphological variation than more proximal limb elements.
source: Results are consistent with the hypothesis that late developing distal bones display greater morphological variation than more proximal limb elements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's results in relation to a developmental hypothesis.

claim: The higher integration observed within the autopod deviates from developmental predictions.
source: However, the higher integration observed within the autopod deviates from such developmental predictions, suggesting that functional specialization plays an important role in driving within-element covariation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study that contradicts the developmental hypothesis.

claim: Functional specialization plays an important role in driving within-element covariation in the autopod.
source: However, the higher integration observed within the autopod deviates from such developmental predictions, suggesting that functional specialization plays an important role in driving within-element covariation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings, suggesting a functional explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: Proximal and distal limb segments show different macroevolutionary patterns.
source: Proximal and distal limb segments also show different macroevolutionary patterns, albeit not showing a perfect proximo-distal gradient.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's macroevolutionary analyses.

claim: Proximal and distal limb segments do not show a perfect proximo-distal gradient in macroevolutionary patterns.
source: Proximal and distal limb segments also show different macroevolutionary patterns, albeit not showing a perfect proximo-distal gradient.
evidence: This is a finding from the study that qualifies the nature of the observed differences.

claim: The high disparity of the mammalian autopod is consistent with the higher potential of development to generate variation in more distal limb structures.
source: The high disparity of the mammalian autopod, reported here, is consistent with the higher potential of development to generate variation in more distal limb structures, as well as functional specialization of the distal elements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in relation to developmental mechanisms.

claim: The high disparity of the mammalian autopod is consistent with functional specialization of the distal elements.
source: The high disparity of the mammalian autopod, reported here, is consistent with the higher potential of development to generate variation in more distal limb structures, as well as functional specialization of the distal elements.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in relation to functional mechanisms.

claim: The evolutionary origin of limbs sets the stage for the remarkable ecological diversity of Tetrapoda.
source: The evolutionary origin of limbs sets the stage for the remarkable ecological diversity of Tetrapoda (Shubin et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shubin et al., 1997.

claim: Limb formation is intrinsically integrated with and constrained by the determination of the tetrapod body plan.
source: From delicate wings to powerful excavating claws, from slender hooved legs to wide flattened flippers, limb formation is intrinsically integrated with and constrained by the determination of the tetrapod body plan (Raff, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Raff, 1996.

claim: The tetrapod limb is typically composed of three basic components: the proximal stylopod (upper arm and thigh), the intermediate zeugopod (lower arm and calf), and the distal autopod (hand and foot).
source: The tetrapod limb is typically composed of three basic components: the proximal stylopod (upper arm and thigh), the intermediate zeugopod (lower arm and calf), and the distal autopod (hand and foot).
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge about tetrapod limb structure.

claim: The proximal to distal organization of limb segments is correlated with their respective evolutionary appearance.
source: The proximal to distal organization of segments is correlated with their respective evolutionary appearance, the stylopod being the first structure to evolve, later followed by the zeugopod, and finally the autopod (Shubin et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shubin et al., 1997.

claim: The stylopod was the first limb structure to evolve, later followed by the zeugopod, and finally the autopod.
source: The proximal to distal organization of segments is correlated with their respective evolutionary appearance, the stylopod being the first structure to evolve, later followed by the zeugopod, and finally the autopod (Shubin et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Shubin et al., 1997.

claim: The three-segment pattern is conserved among quadruped tetrapods.
source: Although the three-segment pattern is conserved among quadruped tetrapods, the morphology of these structures along the proximo-distal axis may evolve differently among groups (Cooper et al., 2011; Galis et al., 2001; Holder, 1983; Sears et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The morphology of limb structures along the proximo-distal axis may evolve differently among groups.
source: Although the three-segment pattern is conserved among quadruped tetrapods, the morphology of these structures along the proximo-distal axis may evolve differently among groups (Cooper et al., 2011; Galis et al., 2001; Holder, 1983; Sears et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Limbs are often studied for their exceptional morphological and ecological diversity.
source: Limbs are often studied for their exceptional morphological and ecological diversity (Chen and Wilson, 2015; Grizante et al., 2010; Kohlsdorf et al., 2001; Ledbetter and Bonett, 2019; Polly, 2007; Rothier et al., 2022; Rothier et al., 2017; Stepanova and Womack, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In mammals, the forelimb is present in all species.
source: In mammals, for example, the forelimb is present in all species and is typically more variable than the hind limb, possibly due to its greater number of functional roles (Figure 1; Polly, 2007; Schmidt and Fischer, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement of fact about mammalian anatomy.

claim: In mammals, the forelimb is typically more variable than the hind limb.
source: In mammals, for example, the forelimb is present in all species and is typically more variable than the hind limb, possibly due to its greater number of functional roles (Figure 1; Polly, 2007; Schmidt and Fischer, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Polly, 2007 and Schmidt and Fischer, 2009.

claim: The greater variability of the mammalian forelimb compared to the hind limb is possibly due to its greater number of functional roles.
source: In mammals, for example, the forelimb is present in all species and is typically more variable than the hind limb, possibly due to its greater number of functional roles (Figure 1; Polly, 2007; Schmidt and Fischer, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: The meristic composition of tetrapod forelimb segments varies along the proximo-distal limb axis.
source: The meristic composition of tetrapod forelimb segments varies along the proximo-distal limb axis, where the autopod exhibits most of the diversity in terms of the number and position of skeletal elements (i.e. fusion and loss of carpal and tarsal bones and alteration of the phalangeal formula; Cooper et al., 2007; Hamrick, 2001; Holder, 1983; Luo et al., 2015; Saxena et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The autopod exhibits most of the diversity in terms of the number and position of skeletal elements.
source: The meristic composition of tetrapod forelimb segments varies along the proximo-distal limb axis, where the autopod exhibits most of the diversity in terms of the number and position of skeletal elements (i.e. fusion and loss of carpal and tarsal bones and alteration of the phalangeal formula; Cooper et al., 2007; Hamrick, 2001; Holder, 1983; Luo et al., 2015; Saxena et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The meristic composition of proximal segments is much more conserved than that of the autopod.
source: Except for lineages that have undergone complete limb loss such as snakes and caecilians, the meristic composition of proximal segments is much more conserved than that of the autopod, displaying some but less frequent cases of element reduction and partial fusion of the zeugopod bones (observed in anurans, bats, manatees, horses, etc., Holder, 1983; Keeffe and Blackburn, 2022; Sears et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Most of the morphological variation observed in the limbs results from changes in the shape and relative size of individual elements without changing the numbers of elements.
source: Although this meristic information is useful to quantify major evolutionary changes in element composition, most of the morphological variation observed in the limbs results from changes in the shape and relative size of individual elements (i.e. variation of form) without changing the numbers of elements, and is often associated with functional adaptation (Fabre et al., 2013; Fabre et al., 2015; Janis and Martín-Serra, 2020; Lungmus and Angielczyk, 2021; Maier et al., 2017; Sears et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Morphological variation in limbs is often associated with functional adaptation.
source: Although this meristic information is useful to quantify major evolutionary changes in element composition, most of the morphological variation observed in the limbs results from changes in the shape and relative size of individual elements (i.e. variation of form) without changing the numbers of elements, and is often associated with functional adaptation (Fabre et al., 2013; Fabre et al., 2015; Janis and Martín-Serra, 2020; Lungmus and Angielczyk, 2021; Maier et al., 2017; Sears et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: It remains unclear how macroevolutionary variation of form is partitioned between the three limb segments.
source: Despite its importance, it remains unclear how this macroevolutionary variation of form is partitioned between the three limb segments.
evidence: This is a statement identifying a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Both functional and developmental factors predict that distal elements should show greater variation of form than more proximal elements.
source: Both functional and developmental factors predict that distal elements should show greater variation of form than more proximal elements.
evidence: This is a statement of theoretical predictions based on functional and developmental biology.

claim: Developmental mechanisms predict greater variation in distal elements due to the timing and spatial structure of morphogenesis.
source: Developmental mechanisms predict this pattern due to the timing and spatial structure of morphogenesis, which has been suggested to influence the macroevolutionary outcome of adult morphologies, including that of the skull (Bardua et al., 2021; Fabre et al., 2020), the vertebrae (Adler et al., 2022), and the limbs (Holder, 1983; Stepanova and Womack, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The timing and spatial structure of morphogenesis has been suggested to influence the macroevolutionary outcome of adult morphologies.
source: Developmental mechanisms predict this pattern due to the timing and spatial structure of morphogenesis, which has been suggested to influence the macroevolutionary outcome of adult morphologies, including that of the skull (Bardua et al., 2021; Fabre et al., 2020), the vertebrae (Adler et al., 2022), and the limbs (Holder, 1983; Stepanova and Womack, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each limb initiates as a bud that extends from the body wall.
source: Each limb initiates as a bud that extends from the body wall and where skeletal elements are generally specified in a proximal to distal sequence that matches their evolutionary appearance during tetrapod origins: development begins with the stylopod, followed by the zeugopod, and terminating in the autopod at the distal end (Figure 2A; Schneider and Shubin, 2013; Shubin et al., 1997; Stopper and Wagner, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Skeletal elements in the limb are generally specified in a proximal to distal sequence that matches their evolutionary appearance during tetrapod origins.
source: Each limb initiates as a bud that extends from the body wall and where skeletal elements are generally specified in a proximal to distal sequence that matches their evolutionary appearance during tetrapod origins: development begins with the stylopod, followed by the zeugopod, and terminating in the autopod at the distal end (Figure 2A; Schneider and Shubin, 2013; Shubin et al., 1997; Stopper and Wagner, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Limb development begins with the stylopod, followed by the zeugopod, and terminating in the autopod at the distal end.
source: Each limb initiates as a bud that extends from the body wall and where skeletal elements are generally specified in a proximal to distal sequence that matches their evolutionary appearance during tetrapod origins: development begins with the stylopod, followed by the zeugopod, and terminating in the autopod at the distal end (Figure 2A; Schneider and Shubin, 2013; Shubin et al., 1997; Stopper and Wagner, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Different mammal species have more similar forelimb morphology during early development, and become more disparate during later stages of morphogenesis.
source: Limb development has been notably studied in mammals, revealing that different species have more similar forelimb morphology during early development, and become more disparate during later stages of morphogenesis (Ross et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ross et al., 2013.

claim: Gene expression of different mammal species is more conserved during early phases of limb development, compared to later phases.
source: Likewise, gene expression of different mammal species is more conserved during early phases of limb development, compared to later phases (Maier et al., 2017), and these patterns might reflect the intrinsic temporal properties of embryogenesis (Galis et al., 2001; Sears et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Maier et al., 2017.

claim: The patterns of gene expression conservation might reflect the intrinsic temporal properties of embryogenesis.
source: Likewise, gene expression of different mammal species is more conserved during early phases of limb development, compared to later phases (Maier et al., 2017), and these patterns might reflect the intrinsic temporal properties of embryogenesis (Galis et al., 2001; Sears et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: The timing of development has been suggested to impact the uneven diversity and evolution of limb segments in frogs.
source: The timing of development has been already suggested to impact the uneven diversity and evolution of limb segments in frogs, with distal, late-developing bones being more variable and tending to diversify faster than proximal, early-forming elements (Stepanova and Womack, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stepanova and Womack, 2020.

claim: In frogs, distal, late-developing bones are more variable and tend to diversify faster than proximal, early-forming elements.
source: The timing of development has been already suggested to impact the uneven diversity and evolution of limb segments in frogs, with distal, late-developing bones being more variable and tending to diversify faster than proximal, early-forming elements (Stepanova and Womack, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stepanova and Womack, 2020.

claim: Early developmental processes mediating the initial specification of structures are generally more constrained than those governing later events.
source: Indeed, early developmental processes mediating the initial specification of structures are generally more constrained than those governing later events, such as organ specialization (Kalinka and Tomancak, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kalinka and Tomancak, 2012.

claim: Because limb development proceeds proximo-to-distally, developmental perturbations at later phases may tend to accumulate higher morphological variation in distal elements.
source: Therefore, because limb development proceeds proximo-to-distally, developmental perturbations at later phases may tend to accumulate higher morphological variation in distal elements (Hallgrímsson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference based on developmental principles, supported by a citation.

claim: One way to investigate the levels of developmental and functional constraints on adult morphologies is by quantifying the phenotypic integration among traits, inferred from the covariation between structures.
source: One way to investigate the levels of developmental and functional constraints on adult morphologies is by quantifying the phenotypic integration among traits, inferred from the covariation between structures.
evidence: This is a methodological statement based on established principles in evolutionary biology.

claim: The fore and hind limbs share genetic and developmental processes that give rise to strong phenotypic integration between and within the limbs.
source: For example, because the fore and hind limbs are serially homologous, they share genetic and developmental processes that give rise to strong phenotypic integration between and within the limbs (Ruvinsky and Gibson-Brown, 2000; Young and Hallgrímsson, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: In mammals, the correlation between homologous limb segments of the fore- and hind limbs suggests that proximal segments are highly integrated to each other.
source: In mammals, the correlation between homologous limb segments of the fore- and hind limbs (i.e. humerus with femur, radius with tibia, metacarpal with metatarsal) suggests that proximal segments are highly integrated to each other (Hallgrímsson et al., 2002; Schmidt and Fischer, 2009; Young and Hallgrímsson, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The more distal elements of the hand and foot show more variable patterns of integration.
source: In contrast, the more distal elements of the hand and foot show more variable patterns of integration, which may reflect functional specialization and the accumulation of variation during later phases of development (Hallgrímsson et al., 2002; Rolian, 2009; Young and Hallgrímsson, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The variable patterns of integration in distal elements may reflect functional specialization and the accumulation of variation during later phases of development.
source: In contrast, the more distal elements of the hand and foot show more variable patterns of integration, which may reflect functional specialization and the accumulation of variation during later phases of development (Hallgrímsson et al., 2002; Rolian, 2009; Young and Hallgrímsson, 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: The patterns and pace of morphological evolution might not be the same between proximal and distal segments.
source: A consequence for limb diversification is that the patterns and pace of morphological evolution might not be the same between proximal and distal segments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of integration patterns.

claim: The study uses a comprehensive data set of 638 species, capturing over 85% of Mammalia family-level diversity.
source: Here, we investigate the evolutionary patterns underlying the morphological diversification of mammalian forelimb segments along a proximal-to-distal axis, using a comprehensive data set of 638 species, capturing over 85% of Mammalia family-level diversity (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's dataset.

claim: Mammals are an ideal group to address questions about limb evolution given their exceptional morphological and ecological diversity.
source: Mammals are an ideal group to address this question given their exceptional morphological and ecological diversity, combined with a substantial literature on the functional variation and the evolutionary development of their limbs (Figure 1; Chen and Wilson, 2015; Grossnickle and Newham, 2016; Howenstine et al., 2021; Lungmus and Angielczyk, 2021; Maier et al., 2017; Polly, 2007; Sears et al., 2007; Weisbecker, 2011; Weisbecker et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The study examined the diversification of limb skeletal elements by quantifying morphological diversity and integration using linear measurements of four forelimb bones.
source: We examined the diversification of limb skeletal elements by quantifying morphological diversity and integration using linear measurements of four forelimb bones (Figure 2B–E, Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodology.

claim: The study estimated the macroevolutionary patterns of limb elements using multivariate phylogenetic comparative methods.
source: We also estimated the macroevolutionary patterns of these elements using multivariate phylogenetic comparative methods.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodology.

claim: This is the first time that the evolutionary patterns observed in the form of proximal versus distal limb elements are investigated using a broad phylogenetic and ecological sample of mammals.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first time that the evolutionary patterns observed in the form of proximal versus distal limb elements are investigated using a broad phylogenetic and ecological sample of mammals, essential to address these questions.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Among the three different evolutionary models examined (Brownian motion, Early-Burst and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck), the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process is the one that better predicts the pattern of evolution for all bones measured.
source: Among the three different evolutionary models examined (Brownian motion, Early-Burst and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck), the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU; see Hansen, 1997) process is the one that better predicts the pattern of evolution for all bones measured (Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's model comparison analyses.

claim: Morphological variation increases along the proximo-distal axis, consistent with the timing of limb condensation during development.
source: Determinants and traces of matrices offer different but complementary generalized metrics to describe the variation of multidimensional data. The matrix trace provides information about the accumulated trait variance, whereas the determinant provides information about the volume occupied by the multivariate data. Both show similar patterns, in which morphological variation increases along the proximo-distal axis, consistent with the timing of limb condensation during development (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and figures.

claim: The early-condensing humerus is the least variable structure (determinant = 0.0015, trace = 0.0079).
source: The early-condensing humerus is the least variable structure (determinant = 0.0015, trace = 0.0079), and the late-condensing phalanx is the most diverse element measured (determinant = 0.0019, trace = 0.0135), followed by the third metacarpal (determinant = 0.0017, trace = 0.0101, Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: The late-condensing phalanx is the most diverse element measured (determinant = 0.0019, trace = 0.0135).
source: The early-condensing humerus is the least variable structure (determinant = 0.0015, trace = 0.0079), and the late-condensing phalanx is the most diverse element measured (determinant = 0.0019, trace = 0.0135), followed by the third metacarpal (determinant = 0.0017, trace = 0.0101, Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: The third metacarpal has a determinant of 0.0017 and trace of 0.0101.
source: The early-condensing humerus is the least variable structure (determinant = 0.0015, trace = 0.0079), and the late-condensing phalanx is the most diverse element measured (determinant = 0.0019, trace = 0.0135), followed by the third metacarpal (determinant = 0.0017, trace = 0.0101, Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: All pairwise comparisons between elements are significant for morphological diversity.
source: All pairwise comparisons between elements are significant (Table 1), although the differences of the determinant distributions of the radius and the metacarpal (p=0.017) are smaller than when using the trace results (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: The differences of the determinant distributions of the radius and the metacarpal (p=0.017) are smaller than when using the trace results (p<0.001).
source: All pairwise comparisons between elements are significant (Table 1), although the differences of the determinant distributions of the radius and the metacarpal (p=0.017) are smaller than when using the trace results (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: Integration is stronger for distal elements compared to proximal ones.
source: Integration, inferred here by the values of eigenvalue dispersion, is stronger for distal elements compared to proximal ones, the phalanx being the most integrated element, followed by the metacarpal (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and figures.

claim: The phalanx is the most integrated element, followed by the metacarpal.
source: Integration, inferred here by the values of eigenvalue dispersion, is stronger for distal elements compared to proximal ones, the phalanx being the most integrated element, followed by the metacarpal (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and figures.

claim: The values of integration do not progressively increase along the proximo-distal axis.
source: The values of integration do not progressively increase along the proximo-distal axis. Instead, the radius is the least integrated structure, and the more proximal humerus is the second least integrated trait.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The radius is the least integrated structure.
source: The values of integration do not progressively increase along the proximo-distal axis. Instead, the radius is the least integrated structure, and the more proximal humerus is the second least integrated trait.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The humerus is the second least integrated trait.
source: The values of integration do not progressively increase along the proximo-distal axis. Instead, the radius is the least integrated structure, and the more proximal humerus is the second least integrated trait.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: All pairwise comparisons between elements are significant for integration.
source: All pairwise comparisons between elements are significant (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: The stationary variances are significantly higher for distal elements compared to proximal ones.
source: The stationary variances are significantly higher for distal elements compared to proximal ones. The metacarpal shows the highest stationary variance, followed by the phalanx (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and figures.

claim: The metacarpal shows the highest stationary variance, followed by the phalanx.
source: The stationary variances are significantly higher for distal elements compared to proximal ones. The metacarpal shows the highest stationary variance, followed by the phalanx (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and figures.

claim: There are no significant differences in the stationary variances at which the humerus and the radius evolve.
source: There are no significant differences in the stationary variances at which the humerus and the radius evolve, these values being significantly lower than those of the two autopodial elements (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: The stationary variances of the humerus and radius are significantly lower than those of the two autopodial elements.
source: There are no significant differences in the stationary variances at which the humerus and the radius evolve, these values being significantly lower than those of the two autopodial elements (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: The results do not support the idea of a proximo-distal gradient of increasing stationary variances.
source: Thus, whereas these results are in line with the predictions of the developmental hypothesis in showing greater evolutionary lability in the distal elements, they do not support the idea of a proximo-distal gradient of increasing stationary variances.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Distal elements such as phalanges and metacarpals are in general more disparate and show greater evolutionary lability than more proximal elements such as the humerus and radius.
source: Based on linear measurements of limb bones we show a general pattern of morphological diversity in Mammalia in which distal elements such as phalanges and metacarpals are in general more disparate and show greater evolutionary lability, as indicated by our measures of stationary variance, than more proximal elements such as the humerus and radius.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main findings.

claim: Developmental constraints imposed by early versus late morphogenesis do not seem to determine differences in within-bone integration.
source: Conversely, developmental constraints imposed by early versus late morphogenesis do not seem to determine differences in within-bone integration; we found that the latest-condensing elements of the hand are more integrated than the earlier-condensing humerus and radius.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The latest-condensing elements of the hand are more integrated than the earlier-condensing humerus and radius.
source: Conversely, developmental constraints imposed by early versus late morphogenesis do not seem to determine differences in within-bone integration; we found that the latest-condensing elements of the hand are more integrated than the earlier-condensing humerus and radius.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The degree of functional specialization across segments might play a role on the levels of within-element integration.
source: We hypothesize that the degree of functional specialization across segments might play a role on the levels of within-element integration, with the autopod potentially being more specialized and therefore exhibiting greater integration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: The autopod is potentially more specialized and therefore exhibits greater integration.
source: We hypothesize that the degree of functional specialization across segments might play a role on the levels of within-element integration, with the autopod potentially being more specialized and therefore exhibiting greater integration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Distal elements evolve, on average, with greater stationary variances (i.e. faster) than the proximal limb elements.
source: We further show that distal elements evolve, on average, with greater stationary variances (i.e. faster) than the proximal limb elements.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: A pattern of increased morphological diversity along the proximal-distal limb axis is consistent with the prediction that lower proximal diversity might have been driven by developmental canalization.
source: A pattern of increased morphological diversity along the proximal-distal limb axis is consistent with the prediction that lower proximal diversity might have been driven by developmental canalization (Hallgrímsson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in relation to developmental theory, supported by a citation.

claim: A similar pattern of increased distal diversity has been previously documented for anurans.
source: A similar pattern has been previously documented for anurans, in a study that compared shape variation of the humerus and the radioulna of the forelimb, as well as the femur, the tibiofibula, and the tarsus of the hind limb (Stepanova and Womack, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stepanova and Womack, 2020.

claim: In anurans, late developing distal structures are not only more diverse but also evolve faster than the most proximal elements belonging to the stylopod.
source: Although this study did not include the digital elements of the hand (metacarpals and phalanges), it showed that late developing distal structures are not only more diverse but also evolve faster than the most proximal elements belonging to the stylopod (Stepanova and Womack, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stepanova and Womack, 2020.

claim: In anurans, microhabitat use explains more shape variation in the distal elements compared to the most proximal limb bones.
source: Microhabitat use also explains more shape variation in the distal elements compared to the most proximal limb bones, suggesting that functional specialization evolves differently along the proximo-distal limb axis (Stepanova and Womack, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Stepanova and Womack, 2020.

claim: The proximal-distal gradient of variation in limb structures may consist of an early conserved pattern shared across tetrapods.
source: Combined with our results, these findings provide evidence that the proximal-distal gradient of variation in limb structures may consist of an early conserved pattern shared across tetrapods, supporting the hypothesis that the timing of development affects the intrinsic capacity of an organism to generate variation and facilitate subsequent functional diversification.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings combined with prior research.

claim: The timing of development affects the intrinsic capacity of an organism to generate variation and facilitate subsequent functional diversification.
source: Combined with our results, these findings provide evidence that the proximal-distal gradient of variation in limb structures may consist of an early conserved pattern shared across tetrapods, supporting the hypothesis that the timing of development affects the intrinsic capacity of an organism to generate variation and facilitate subsequent functional diversification.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the study's findings and prior research.

claim: Functional variation is often a good predictor of the pattern of morphological variation of limb bones.
source: Functional variation is often a good predictor of the pattern of morphological variation of limb bones (Chen and Wilson, 2015; Fabre et al., 2013; Grossnickle et al., 2020; Weaver and Grossnickle, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The autopod is the structure that interacts directly with the surrounding environment.
source: The autopod is the structure that interacts directly with the surrounding environment, performing important activities such as providing support to the body during locomotion and, in some cases, digging, handling food, grooming, and mediating social interactions (Biewener and Patek, 2018; Mc Grew et al., 2001; Naghizadeh et al., 2020; Sustaita et al., 2013; Weisbecker and Warton, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The hand bones are subjected to more dynamic selective pressures that ultimately favour greater diversity and evolutionary lability compared to proximal segments.
source: Our results corroborate the idea that the hand bones are subjected to more dynamic selective pressures that ultimately favour greater diversity and evolutionary lability compared to proximal segments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Few studies have quantified the functional relationships driving autopod variation in mammals.
source: However, few studies have quantified the functional relationships driving autopod variation in mammals (Almécija et al., 2015; Rolian, 2009; Weisbecker and Schmid, 2007; Weisbecker and Warton, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The study comprises the most comprehensive taxonomic dataset on the forearm morphology of mammals.
source: To our knowledge, our study comprises the most comprehensive taxonomic dataset on the forearm morphology of mammals.
evidence: This is a claim about the scope of the study's dataset.

claim: The use of linear measurements succeeded at establishing comparable topological distances and provided a robust overview for the global morphological diversity between limb segments across the mammalian tree of life.
source: The use of linear measurements succeeded at establishing comparable topological distances and provided a robust overview for the global morphological diversity between limb segments across the mammalian tree of life.
evidence: This is an assessment of the study's methodological approach.

claim: The linear measurement method imposes some limitations on capturing detailed local shape variation.
source: However, this method imposes some limitations on capturing detailed local shape variation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of methodological limitations.

claim: The proximal joint at the humerus can encompass complex surfaces which determine the mobility of the limb.
source: For example, the proximal joint at the humerus can encompass complex surfaces which determine the mobility of the limb (Arias-Martorell, 2019; Veeger and Veeger and van der Helm, 2007), but variation therein is not captured by our measurements.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Variation in the proximal joint of the humerus is not captured by the study's measurements.
source: For example, the proximal joint at the humerus can encompass complex surfaces which determine the mobility of the limb (Arias-Martorell, 2019; Veeger and Veeger and van der Helm, 2007), but variation therein is not captured by our measurements.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of methodological limitations.

claim: The shape and size of the deltopectoral crest of the humerus may display considerable interspecific variation.
source: Likewise, the shape and size of the deltopectoral crest of the humerus may display considerable interspecific variation (Chen and Wilson, 2015; Hopkins and Davis, 2009; Samuels and Van Valkenburgh, 2008), and is also not quantified here.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The deltopectoral crest variation is not quantified in the study.
source: Likewise, the shape and size of the deltopectoral crest of the humerus may display considerable interspecific variation (Chen and Wilson, 2015; Hopkins and Davis, 2009; Samuels and Van Valkenburgh, 2008), and is also not quantified here.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of methodological limitations.

claim: Previous studies that have incorporated complex geometric surfaces of the long bones detected that the robustness is one of the principal factors contributing to the pattern of morphological variation.
source: Either way, previous studies that have incorporated complex geometric surfaces of the long bones detected that the robustness (i.e., the correlation of length and thickness) is one of the principal factors contributing to the pattern of morphological variation (Fabre et al., 2017; Fabre et al., 2014; Michaud et al., 2020), consistent with our results.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The ulna is highly variable, with the olecranon particularly being a strong predictor of locomotor habit.
source: The ulna is highly variable, with the olecranon particularly being a strong predictor of locomotor habit (Chen and Wilson, 2015; Lungmus and Angielczyk, 2021; Milne and Granatosky, 2021; Samuels and Van Valkenburgh, 2008; Van Valkenburgh, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The ulna is distally reduced or fused to the radius in many taxa.
source: However, due to the high variation of the ulna, the topological distances used to describe the skeletal morphology (length, width, and height) cannot be applied to this bone in all species as the ulna is distally reduced or fused to the radius in many taxa (Sears et al., 2007), thus preventing us from quantifying the diversity between this and other limb bones.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sears et al., 2007.

claim: The high integration detected in the mammalian hand suggests that developmental constraints of early versus late bone condensation do not predict within-element covariation.
source: The high integration detected in the mammalian hand suggests that developmental constraints of early versus late bone condensation do not predict within-element covariation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: In the matter of relative bone integration, the timing of condensation is unable to predict which elements are the most and the least integrated.
source: Yet, in the matter of relative bone integration, the timing of condensation is unable predict which elements are the most and the least integrated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The proximal and distal humeral joints perform different functions and allow very different movements.
source: The proximal and distal humeral joints perform different functions and allow very different movements: the proximal head connects the limb to the pectoral girdle at the shoulder through a complex ball-and-socket articulation (Arias-Martorell, 2019; Veeger and Veeger and van der Helm, 2007), and it distally articulates with the ulna and the radius at the elbow driving forelimb mobility and stability (Fabre et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The proximal head of the humerus connects the limb to the pectoral girdle at the shoulder through a complex ball-and-socket articulation.
source: The proximal and distal humeral joints perform different functions and allow very different movements: the proximal head connects the limb to the pectoral girdle at the shoulder through a complex ball-and-socket articulation (Arias-Martorell, 2019; Veeger and Veeger and van der Helm, 2007), and it distally articulates with the ulna and the radius at the elbow driving forelimb mobility and stability (Fabre et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The humerus distally articulates with the ulna and the radius at the elbow driving forelimb mobility and stability.
source: The proximal and distal humeral joints perform different functions and allow very different movements: the proximal head connects the limb to the pectoral girdle at the shoulder through a complex ball-and-socket articulation (Arias-Martorell, 2019; Veeger and Veeger and van der Helm, 2007), and it distally articulates with the ulna and the radius at the elbow driving forelimb mobility and stability (Fabre et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The radial joints are involved in different functions, having a proximal head connected to the elbow and an enlarged distal extremity articulated at the wrist with carpals and sometimes the ulna.
source: The radial joints are also involved in different functions, having a proximal head connected to the elbow and an enlarged distal extremity articulated at the wrist with carpals and sometimes the ulna (MacLeod and Rose, 1993; Polly, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The articular surfaces of long bones are differently impacted by functional specialization related to locomotor habit.
source: Because they are involved in different functions, the articular surfaces of long bones are differently impacted by functional specialization related to locomotor habit (Fabre et al., 2014; Lungmus and Angielczyk, 2021; MacLeod and Rose, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The different functional demands at the proximal and distal bone extremities might encompass a reduction of covariation between these traits, as detected for the humerus and the radius.
source: In terms of within-element integration, the different functional demands at the proximal and distal bone extremities might encompass a reduction of covariation between these traits, as detected here for the humerus and the radius.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Phalanges articulate with the metacarpals at a bi-axial-joint (movement at two axes: flexion/extension, abduction/adduction).
source: The metacarpal and the phalangeal articulations, on the other hand, work more similarly: phalanges articulate with the metacarpals at a bi-axial-joint (movement at two axes: flexion/extension, abduction/adduction) and articulate with each other at hinge joints which allow only one axis of movement (flexion and extension; Napier and Tuttle, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Phalanges articulate with each other at hinge joints which allow only one axis of movement (flexion and extension).
source: The metacarpal and the phalangeal articulations, on the other hand, work more similarly: phalanges articulate with the metacarpals at a bi-axial-joint (movement at two axes: flexion/extension, abduction/adduction) and articulate with each other at hinge joints which allow only one axis of movement (flexion and extension; Napier and Tuttle, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The strong integration of hand bones detected for mammals indicates that these elements experience a highly correlated evolution.
source: The strong integration of hand bones detected for mammals indicates that these elements experience a highly correlated evolution, which in this case might also emerge from functional similarity and interdependence at the articulations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The strong integration of hand bones might emerge from functional similarity and interdependence at the articulations.
source: The strong integration of hand bones detected for mammals indicates that these elements experience a highly correlated evolution, which in this case might also emerge from functional similarity and interdependence at the articulations.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: The relationship between integration and morphological variation is not always consistent among traits and taxa.
source: The relationship between integration and morphological variation is not always consistent among traits and taxa (Felice et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Some studies have shown clear positive associations between high integration and phenotypic variation.
source: Whereas some studies have shown clear positive associations between high integration and phenotypic variation (Fabre et al., 2021; Fabre et al., 2020; Randau and Goswami, 2017), negative associations have been also reported (Felice and Goswami, 2018; Goswami and Polly, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Negative associations between integration and phenotypic variation have been reported.
source: Whereas some studies have shown clear positive associations between high integration and phenotypic variation (Fabre et al., 2021; Fabre et al., 2020; Randau and Goswami, 2017), negative associations have been also reported (Felice and Goswami, 2018; Goswami and Polly, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: There is no evidence for a strong correspondence of integration with morphological diversity in proximal forelimb segments.
source: We find no evidence for a strong correspondence of integration with morphological diversity in proximal forelimb segments: the radius exhibits greater diversity of form than the humerus but presents the weakest values of integration among the bones measured.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The radius exhibits greater diversity of form than the humerus but presents the weakest values of integration among the bones measured.
source: We find no evidence for a strong correspondence of integration with morphological diversity in proximal forelimb segments: the radius exhibits greater diversity of form than the humerus but presents the weakest values of integration among the bones measured.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: For the distal elements, the highly integrated autopod, especially the phalanx, also corresponds to the most diverse structure of the limb.
source: For the distal elements, however, our results show that the highly integrated autopod, especially the phalanx, also corresponds to the most diverse structure of the limb (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and figures.

claim: Integration may constrain the evolution of the phenotype to a limited portion of morphospace.
source: Though integration may constrain the evolution of the phenotype to a limited portion of morphospace, it may also promote variation by driving the evolution of these traits in response to selection for functional specialization (Felice et al., 2018; Goswami et al., 2014; Hansen and Houle, 2008; Lande, 1979).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Integration may promote variation by driving the evolution of traits in response to selection for functional specialization.
source: Though integration may constrain the evolution of the phenotype to a limited portion of morphospace, it may also promote variation by driving the evolution of these traits in response to selection for functional specialization (Felice et al., 2018; Goswami et al., 2014; Hansen and Houle, 2008; Lande, 1979).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: High integration in the phalanx and metacarpus possibly favoured the evolution of functionally specialized autopod structures.
source: Such dynamics appear to be observed in the distal elements: high integration in the phalanx and metacarpus, possibly favoured the evolution of functionally specialized autopod structures, contributes to the high variation observed in mammalian hand bones.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The autopodial bones evolve, on average, with greater stationary variances around their optima than the stylopod and the zeugopod.
source: The autopodial bones evolve, on average, with greater stationary variances around their optima than the stylopod and the zeugopod (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and figures.

claim: Evolutionary lability does not increase in a perfect proximal-to-distal pattern.
source: Although the developmental hypothesis predicted that the fastest evolving structures would belong to the late-condensed distal limb, evolutionary lability do not increase in a perfect proximal-to-distal pattern, and the third metacarpal is the structure with the highest stationary variances, followed by the phalanx.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The third metacarpal is the structure with the highest stationary variances, followed by the phalanx.
source: Although the developmental hypothesis predicted that the fastest evolving structures would belong to the late-condensed distal limb, evolutionary lability do not increase in a perfect proximal-to-distal pattern, and the third metacarpal is the structure with the highest stationary variances, followed by the phalanx.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Functional selection combined with the higher potential of development to generate variation in the morphology of more distal limb elements facilitated the evolution of high autopodial disparity in response to varying environmental demands across mammals.
source: These findings suggest that functional selection (resulting from the direct impact of autopodial structures on locomotor performance) combined with the higher potential of development to generate variation in the morphology of more distal limb elements, facilitated the evolution of high autopodial disparity in response to varying environmental demands across mammals.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Notable transformations in the metacarpal and phalangeal morphology are observed in cursorial taxa that present specializations allowing for endurance running.
source: Notable transformations in the metacarpal and phalangeal morphology are observed in cursorial taxa that present specializations allowing for endurance running, typically involving the elongation of the distal limb in relation to proximal segments (Polly, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Cursorial specializations typically involve the elongation of the distal limb in relation to proximal segments.
source: Notable transformations in the metacarpal and phalangeal morphology are observed in cursorial taxa that present specializations allowing for endurance running, typically involving the elongation of the distal limb in relation to proximal segments (Polly, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Morphological adaptations to cursoriality mostly encompass the modification of autopod posture to digitigrady and unguligrady.
source: For example, morphological adaptations to cursoriality mostly encompass the modification of autopod posture to digitigrady (animals that stand on the distal ends of metapodials and middle phalanges, such as cats and dogs) and unguligrady (animals that stand on their hooved distal-most phalanx, such as horses and cows; Clifford, 2010; Polly, 2007; Wang, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Digitigrady is observed in many carnivorans providing limb elongation and thus increasing stride length.
source: Digitigrady is observed in many carnivorans providing limb elongation and thus increasing stride length (Polly, 2007; Wang, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Extant horses exhibit one of the most dramatic modifications of the third metapodial and phalanges among all unguligrade taxa.
source: Extant horses exhibit one of the most dramatic modifications of the third metapodial and phalanges among all unguligrade taxa: the limb is uniquely supported by the third toe, which is considerably enlarged and elongated, whilst the lateral fingers are markedly reduced (McHorse et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: In horses, the limb is uniquely supported by the third toe, which is considerably enlarged and elongated, whilst the lateral fingers are markedly reduced.
source: Extant horses exhibit one of the most dramatic modifications of the third metapodial and phalanges among all unguligrade taxa: the limb is uniquely supported by the third toe, which is considerably enlarged and elongated, whilst the lateral fingers are markedly reduced (McHorse et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Evolutionary transitions in foot and hand postures are associated with strong selection for rapid changes in increasing body size.
source: One recent study suggested that the evolutionary transitions in foot and hand postures are associated with strong selection for rapid changes in increasing body size (Kubo et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Body size is positively associated with the tempo of evolution of postcranial morphology in both ground and tree dwelling animals.
source: For example, body size is positively associated with the tempo of evolution of postcranial morphology (hand and foot bones included) in both ground and tree dwelling animals, where medium-sized animals tend to exhibit higher stationary variances than small-sized species (Weaver and Grossnickle, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Medium-sized animals tend to exhibit higher stationary variances than small-sized species.
source: For example, body size is positively associated with the tempo of evolution of postcranial morphology (hand and foot bones included) in both ground and tree dwelling animals, where medium-sized animals tend to exhibit higher stationary variances than small-sized species (Weaver and Grossnickle, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Functional specializations related to locomotion and size likely played a role in driving the morphological evolution of the limb.
source: Overall, these examples suggest that functional specializations related to the locomotion and size likely played a role in driving the morphological evolution of the limb, potentially driving the accelerated evolution of hand bone morphology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the examples discussed.

claim: Functional specializations potentially drove the accelerated evolution of hand bone morphology.
source: Overall, these examples suggest that functional specializations related to the locomotion and size likely played a role in driving the morphological evolution of the limb, potentially driving the accelerated evolution of hand bone morphology.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the examples discussed.

claim: This study uses a macroevolutionary framework to compare the general patterns of form diversification of proximal and distal limb elements in mammals for the first time.
source: This study uses a macroevolutionary framework to compare, for the first time, the general patterns of form diversification of proximal and distal limb elements in mammals.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: The evolution of the mammalian forelimb involves different patterns of morphological diversification when comparing limb segments along a proximal–distal gradient.
source: Our results reveal that the evolution of the mammalian forelimb involves different patterns of morphological diversification when comparing limb segments along a proximal–distal gradient.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main findings.

claim: The diversification of autopodial elements was much more dynamic than that of the zeugopod and stylopod.
source: We detected that the diversification of autopodial elements was much more dynamic than that of the zeugopod and stylopod, involving higher morphological diversity, stronger integration, and greater evolutionary lability at distal structures.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main findings.

claim: The late-condensing distal elements such as metacarpals and phalanges exhibit higher morphological diversity than early-condensing, more proximal, elements.
source: Specifically, we corroborate the premise that the late-condensing distal elements such as metacarpals and phalanges (in the autopod) exhibit higher morphological diversity than early-condensing, more proximal, elements.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main findings.

claim: The pattern of higher distal diversity might emerge from different levels of constraints during the developmental succession.
source: This pattern might emerge from different levels of constraints during the developmental succession.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The strong integration of the autopodial elements most likely reflects the functional similarity and interdependence between joints in response to functional demands.
source: Particularly, the strong integration of the autopodial elements most likely reflects the functional similarity and interdependence between joints in response to functional demands.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The study sampled 638 species of mammals (670 specimens), representing 598 genera of 138 living families.
source: We sampled 638 species of mammals (670 specimens), representing 598 genera of 138 living families (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's sampling.

claim: Sampling varies from one to four individuals per genus.
source: Sampling varies from one to four individuals per genus.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's sampling.

claim: The study provided micro-CT-scans and surface scans of 58 small to medium sized-specimens from different institutions.
source: We provided micro-CT-scans and surface scans of 58 small to medium sized-specimens from different institutions (available online at MorphoSource.org, Supplementary file 1), 23 of them previously used by Martín-Serra and Benson, 2020.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's data sources.

claim: The digital dataset was combined with 351 meshes available on MorphoSource.org.
source: The digital dataset was combined with 351 meshes available on MorphoSource.org (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's data sources.

claim: The dataset was complemented with measurements provided by caliper of 261 medium to large body-sized species from the mammal collection of the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle.
source: We complemented this dataset with measurements provided by caliper of 261 medium to large body-sized species from the mammal collection of the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle (Paris, France; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's data sources.

claim: The study measured 20 linear distances from anterior limb bones, including the humerus, the radius, the third metacarpal and the first phalanx of digit III.
source: We measured 20 linear distances from anterior limb bones, including the humerus, the radius, the third metacarpal and the first phalanx of digit III.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's measurements.

claim: Five measurements were acquired for each element: length, widths (proximal, mid-shaft and distal) and height.
source: We acquired five measurements for each element: length, widths (proximal, mid-shaft and distal) and height (Figure 2, see detailed description in Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's measurements.

claim: The ulna was not included because this bone is fused to the radius in many taxa.
source: We opted not to include the ulna because this bone is fused to the radius in many taxa (see Sears et al., 2007), preventing the acquisition of such measurements.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodological choices, supported by a citation.

claim: The metacarpal and first phalanx of digit III were sampled because this is the only digit present in the hands of all mammalian lineages.
source: The metacarpal and first phalanx of digit III were sampled because this is the only digit present in the hands of all mammalian lineages, even in groups that exhibit digit loss or fusion with other autopodial elements, such as in golden moles and ungulates (Clifford, 2010; McHorse et al., 2019; Prothero, 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodological choices, supported by citations.

claim: Each individual was measured twice with the subsequent calculation of the mean and standard error in order to verify measurement error.
source: Each individual was measured twice with the subsequent calculation of the mean and standard error in order to verify measurement error.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's methodology.

claim: The error estimate was most often below 1.5% regardless of an animal's size and the measurement method.
source: The error estimate was most often below 1.5% regardless of an animal's size and the measurement method, demonstrating consistency and repeatability of the methods employed.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's measurement reliability.

claim: The study assembled the average species body mass of adults from the PanTHERIA database and complemented by literature sources when necessary.
source: Body mass values were rarely available for the individuals measured, so we assembled the average species body mass of adults from the PanTHERIA database (Jones et al., 2009) and complemented by literature sources when necessary (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's data sources.

claim: Species taxonomy followed the Mammal Diversity Database published by Burgin et al., 2018.
source: Species taxonomy followed the Mammal Diversity Database published by Burgin et al., 2018.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's taxonomic framework.

claim: The study used the phangorn R package to estimate a maximum clade credibility tree from a posterior sample of 10,000 trees published by Upham et al., 2019.
source: We used the phangorn R package (Schliep, 2011) to estimate a maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree from a posterior sample of 10,000 trees published by Upham et al., 2019.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's phylogenetic methods.

claim: Allometry generally explains most of morphological variation, as body parts usually grow together.
source: Allometry generally explains most of morphological variation, as body parts usually grow together, masking variation mediated by local development (Marroig, 2007; Raff, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The study removed the allometric component of the dataset in order to reduce variation associated with other sources of development.
source: Because we are particularly interested in understanding morphological constraints imposed by the local development of the limb, we decided to remove the allometric component of our dataset in order to reduce variation associated with other sources of development.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's analytical approach.

claim: The study calculated geometric means as a proxy for body size by including values of the individuals themselves and the average species body mass.
source: We could not retrieve the individual body masses for most of the species included, so we calculated geometric means as a proxy for body size by including values of the individuals themselves and the average species body mass.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's analytical approach.

claim: The study fitted the log10-transformed trait means in a phylogenetic generalized least-squares (PGLS) using the geometric means as a predictor.
source: We calculated the geometric means of all measurements acquired, including the linear scaled body mass, and then we fitted the log10-transformed trait means in a phylogenetic generalized least-squares (PGLS) using the geometric means as a predictor.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's analytical approach.

claim: The study calculated the fit of three models of evolution using LASSO penalization: Brownian Motion (BM), Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU), and Early Burst (EB).
source: We calculated the fit of three models of evolution using LASSO penalization: Brownian Motion (BM), Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU), and Early Burst (EB).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's analytical approach.

claim: The study compared the likelihood of the model fits with Generalized Information Criterion (GIC) to establish which model provided the best fit.
source: We compared the likelihood of the model fits with Generalized Information Criterion (GIC) to establish which model provided the best fit.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's analytical approach.

claim: The study used a parametric bootstrap approach to assess the uncertainty around point estimates for morphological diversity and integration.
source: We used a parametric bootstrap approach to assess the uncertainty around point estimates for morphological diversity and integration.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's analytical approach.

claim: The study simulated 100 datasets for each bone on MCC tree using the OU process fit.
source: We first simulated 100 datasets for each bone on MCC tree using the OU process fit (that is, the best fit model on our original data) with parameters estimates from the empirical regression (function mvSIM() from mvMORPH; Clavel et al., 2015; Clavel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's analytical approach.

claim: The determinant is a scalar measure that summarizes the information contained in a square matrix.
source: The determinant is a scalar measure that summarize the information contained in a square matrix (det(), R Core Team, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement of mathematical definition.

claim: For a covariance matrix, the determinant corresponds to a generalized measure of variance.
source: For a covariance matrix, it corresponds to a generalized measure of variance, because contrary to the trace, the determinant account for the correlations/covariances between the traits (Rencher, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The study calculated the magnitude of integration for each bone separately, based on eigenvalue dispersion in their respective matrices.
source: We calculated the magnitude of integration for each bone separately, based on eigenvalue dispersion in their respective matrices.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's analytical approach.

claim: Highly integrated traits have most of the independent variance concentrated in the first few eigenvalues.
source: For instance, highly integrated traits have most of the independent variance concentrated in the first few eigenvalues, while uncorrelated traits have the variance similarly distributed between eigenvalues (Pavlicev et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Uncorrelated traits have the variance similarly distributed between eigenvalues.
source: For instance, highly integrated traits have most of the independent variance concentrated in the first few eigenvalues, while uncorrelated traits have the variance similarly distributed between eigenvalues (Pavlicev et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The study replicated the body mass linear regressions with 100 randomly sampled trees from Upham et al., 2019 to assess variability due to tree topology and branching times uncertainties.
source: To assess variability due to the tree topology and branching times uncertainties, we replicated the body mass linear regressions with 100 randomly sampled trees from Upham et al., 2019.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's analytical approach.

claim: Under a Brownian motion process, the tempo of evolution can be directly inferred from the σ2.
source: Under a Brownian motion process, the tempo of evolution can be directly inferred from the σ2, which represents the total variance of traits changes linearly, as a function of the traits covariances matrix and time (Harmon, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: In an OU process, traits evolve towards an optimum θ with an attraction α.
source: In an OU process, however, traits evolve towards an optimum θ with an attraction α.
evidence: This is a statement of the OU model definition.

claim: The trait variance changes with time in BM, while it is not related to time in OU when stationary.
source: The main difference between BM and OU, is that the trait variance changes with time in BM, while it is not related to time in OU when stationary (Hunt, 2012).

claim: A comparable rate metric for traits evolving under OU process is the stationary variance (σ2/2α).
